solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Unintended stress to a learner I'd kept in

indicators.note: something kept in is held inside, so the second word sits within the first

parts.note: an accent is stress laid on a syllable
the contraction written without its apostrophe
taken as written
L is the learner driver's plate

explanation.surface: A teacher puts a pupil under pressure without meaning to by keeping them in after school.
explanation.definitionFit: Something accidental happens by chance, without anyone planning or meaning it, so the two words are synonyms.

clue.text: Attending Shakespeare's As You Like It

parts.note: attending a concert is being at it
Will is Shakespeare's first name, William shortened

explanation.surface: A theatregoer goes to see a performance of Shakespeare's comedy.
explanation.walkthrough: The play title looks like part of the theatre outing, but read as plain words it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something at will means doing it whenever and however you please, which is what the comedy's title phrase says.

clue.text: Element, in place of Pope, supporting church

indicators.note: in a down entry a supporting piece holds the other up from below, so it comes second

parts.note: CH is the standard abbreviation for church
the Pope's seat is in Rome

explanation.surface: A churchman takes the Pope's role while backing the Church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In place of' looks like 'instead of', suggesting a substitution, but it means the place where the Pope is.
explanation.definitionFit: Chromium, often called chrome, is a metallic chemical element on the periodic table.

clue.text: Cut off inside, dither disastrously

indicators.note: things that go disastrously are wrecked and jumbled, so the letters are put in a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone trapped indoors hesitates hopelessly and loses contact with the world.
explanation.definitionFit: A child who is disinherited is excluded from a will, which is exactly being cut off by the family.

clue.text: Refusal to authorize safe and secluded place

parts.note: the plain word of refusal
to OK something is to approve it

explanation.surface: An official refuses permission for a safe and quiet hideaway.
explanation.definitionFit: A nook is a sheltered corner or recess, a cosy hidden spot tucked away from view.

clue.text: A new tax on relative, in short? Just the opposite

indicators.note: something put in short is abbreviated, so only a cut-down form of the word is used

parts.note: taken as written
N is the standard abbreviation for new
a tithe is a tenth paid as a levy, historically to the church
a sister is a family relative

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a new tax falls on a relative, and is told the reverse is true.
explanation.walkthrough: SIS is the familiar short form of sister; in a down entry 'on' puts the tax above the relative.
explanation.definitionFit: An antithesis is the direct contrary of something, its exact reverse or polar counterpart.

clue.text: Heated fighting before start of match

parts.note: war is armed fighting

indicators.note: the start of a word is its opening letter, so only that is kept

parts.note: the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: Tempers flare and a scuffle breaks out just before kick-off.
explanation.definitionFit: Something heated has been made warm, so the adjectives overlap as near synonyms for raised temperature.

clue.text: Diagnose wrongly, hence suffered pain

indicators.note: doing something wrongly gets it muddled, so the letters come out in a different order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A doctor gets the illness wrong, so the patient is left in pain.
explanation.definitionFit: To have agonised is to have endured agony, great physical or mental torment.

clue.text: Daisy's family member, silly girl mad about love

indicators.note: about means around, so the jumbled letters wrap round the next piece
silly suggests foolish and scatterbrained, so the letters are scrambled

parts.note: taken as written
love is zero in tennis, shaped like the letter O

explanation.surface: Daisy's relative is a giddy girl who is crazy about romance.
explanation.walkthrough: Daisy reads as a woman's name, but it is the flower: the daisy family, Asteraceae, includes the marigold.
explanation.definitionFit: The marigold is a plant in the daisy family, Asteraceae, so it is a botanical relative of the daisy.

clue.text: The value of one part of speech for poet

parts.note: a word is a single part of speech, and with the possessive it is word's
worth is value

explanation.surface: Someone asks what a single word is worth to a poet.
explanation.walkthrough: The parts are read in reverse order: one word's worth, the value of a word.
explanation.definitionFit: William Wordsworth was the English Romantic poet who wrote about daffodils and the Lake District.

clue.text: Trip with ancient city as destination

parts.note: to marks where you are heading
Ur is the ancient Sumerian city, a crossword regular

explanation.surface: A traveller plans a journey ending at an ancient city's ruins.
explanation.definitionFit: A tour is a journey or excursion taken for pleasure, so it is a synonym for a trip.

clue.text: Inferior example of its type, or real change in medicine?

indicators.note: in means placed within, so the rearranged letters go inside the remedy

parts.note: a potion is a liquid dose of medicine

indicators.note: a change alters the arrangement, so the letters are reordered

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A clue wonders whether a weak specimen needs a genuine change in its treatment.
explanation.definitionFit: A poor relation is something regarded as a lesser, second-rate member of a group compared with its superiors.

clue.text: Regret American getting caught in fast time

indicators.note: something caught in a net is held inside it, so one piece is enclosed by the other

parts.note: Lent is the Christian season of fasting before Easter
AM is a short form of American

explanation.surface: An American is sorry to be caught out during a period of fasting.
explanation.definitionFit: To lament something is to mourn or express sorrow over it, so both verbs mean grieving about it.

clue.text: Rowing at the stern — or fine in part of bow

indicators.note: in means placed within, so one piece is put inside the other

parts.note: an archer's bow is drawn by its string
OK means all right, fine

explanation.surface: A rowing note: rowing at the back of the boat, or taking a place at the front.
explanation.walkthrough: Bow and stern set a boat scene, but the bow here is the archer's weapon. The stroke is the rower nearest the stern who sets the rhythm.
explanation.definitionFit: Stroking a boat means rowing as stroke, the oarsman seated nearest the stern who sets the crew's rate.

clue.text: Where pictures show irritation in blood vessel

indicators.note: in means placed within, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: an artery carries blood from the heart
gall is annoyance or a sore caused by rubbing

explanation.surface: Scans reveal an inflamed blood vessel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pictures show' reads like medical images revealing a problem, but show is a verb about display.
explanation.definitionFit: An art gallery is a building where paintings are put on public display for visitors.

clue.text: Author, ergo, revised repeatedly and skilfully

indicators.note: a text revised again and again is reworked, so the letters, taken twice over, go into a new order

parts.note: 'repeatedly' asks for this word twice over
doing something well is doing it skilfully

explanation.surface: A writer keeps reworking his argument, and does it with great skill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Repeatedly' doubles the Latin word before it is rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: George Orwell was the English writer of Animal Farm and Nineteen Eighty-Four.

clue.text: Ridicule Teddy repeatedly

wordplay.note: Winnie-the-Pooh is the famous teddy bear, named twice over

explanation.surface: A child keeps mocking a teddy bear.
explanation.definitionFit: To pooh-pooh an idea is to dismiss it scornfully, treating it with contempt.

clue.text: To approach young lady, get a close shave

parts.note: to near a place is to approach it
Miss is the title of an unmarried young woman

explanation.surface: A young man smartens himself up with a careful shave before approaching a girl.
explanation.definitionFit: A close shave is an idiom for a narrow escape, just as a near miss is a disaster only just avoided.

clue.text: When local access starts, preparing to read inside stories

parts.note: you begin reading a book by opening it
The Times is a newspaper, full of stories inside

explanation.surface: A reader settles down as the library opens, getting ready to look into its stories.
explanation.walkthrough: A local is a British pub, so local access starts when the pub opens its doors.
explanation.definitionFit: Opening times are the hours at which a pub or shop admits customers each day.

clue.text: Home supporter has little time for young one

parts.note: someone at home is in
a fan supports a team
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: A home fan has barely a moment to spare for a child.
explanation.definitionFit: An infant is a baby or very small child, a little one in its earliest years.

clue.text: Astute and aggressive woman getting diamonds

parts.note: a shrew is a bad-tempered, scolding woman
D is the card-playing abbreviation for diamonds

explanation.surface: A sharp, pushy woman ends up with a fortune in jewels.
explanation.definitionFit: Shrewd describes someone with keen practical judgement, clever and perceptive in dealings.

clue.text: What torments flesh or tail of pony?

definitions.text: What torments flesh or tail of pony

indicators.note: tormenting something twists and wrings it, so the following letters are mangled

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the tail of a word is its final letter, so only that is kept

parts.note: the closing letter of the word

explanation.surface: A riddle asks what pest bites a horse's skin or its tail.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both definition and wordplay: the insect bites horses' flesh and is swished away by the tail.
explanation.definitionFit: The horsefly is a large biting insect that pesters horses and cattle, drawing blood from their skin.

clue.text: Strike outside a corporation

indicators.note: outside means surrounding, so the first word goes round the second

parts.note: to punch is to strike with the fist
taken as written

explanation.surface: Workers walk out on strike at a big company.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strike' and 'corporation' suggest industrial action; corporation is old British slang for a big belly.
explanation.definitionFit: Corporation is a jocular, dated term for a large stomach, the same thing as a pot belly.

clue.text: Like one's local, serving up hard drink

indicators.note: in a down entry, up means read from the bottom, so the pieces run backwards

parts.note: H is the pencil-grade abbreviation for hard
gin is a spirit drink

explanation.surface: Your local pub pours you a stiff drink.
explanation.walkthrough: Local suggests a pub, but here it means close at hand.
explanation.definitionFit: Nigh is an old word for near, and something local is near to where you live.

clue.text: Part of America under control of Columbus

definitions.meaning: first meaning: one of the fifty United States
second meaning: a state governed from its capital city, Columbus

explanation.surface: Part of the New World lies under the sway of its discoverer, Christopher Columbus.
explanation.walkthrough: Columbus suggests the explorer who reached America, but it is the state capital.
explanation.definitionFit: This Midwestern state is part of the United States, and its capital and seat of government is Columbus.

clue.text: To run off with one partner is within the law

parts.note: to leg it is slang for running away
the Roman numeral for one
a mate is a partner

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether eloping with a lover is permitted by law.
explanation.definitionFit: Something legitimate is lawful, permitted by statute and recognised as legal.

clue.text: Person entertaining large crowd

definitions.meaning: first meaning: someone who receives guests
second meaning: a great number, a multitude

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as one person amusing a big audience, but the two halves are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both the giver of a party who welcomes guests and a great multitude of people.

clue.text: Having bars, like well-known watering-holes

definitions.meaning: first meaning: containing short horizontal dashes between words
second meaning: both compound words here are written with a dash joining their parts

explanation.surface: A pub guide praises places with bars, like famous drinking spots.
explanation.walkthrough: Bars and watering-holes suggest pubs; the bars are the short dashes, and the clue's own words show them.
explanation.definitionFit: A compound word written with a joining dash between its parts is spelled with that punctuation mark.
